Well this further proves my theory; Once a controversial (read: critical of Reddit, USA or Israel) post hits the front page from a default, I think the mods are asked to remove it. It is no secret that the mainstream media often collaborate to send out the same message and it is my assertion that Reddit, at ownership level, is being forced to pull itself in line with the rest of the mainstream media. This would explain why posts that ordinarily would be acceptable are pulled for contentious reasons ONLY when they hit the front page.

Amusingly enough reddit is actually and literally owned by companies who also happen to own large chunks of the mainstream media. The parent company of Reddit is Conde Naste. You can verify this from a company description of Conde Naste on a Conde Naste jobs application here. Conde Naste is in turn owned by Advance Publications. Something you can see "disclosed" here. There's a disclosure about a conflict of interest in that article. Try to find it. It's literally in the middle of the second major paragraph in the final section. Quoting the article, "(disclosure: Ars and reddit share a parent company, namely Advance Publications)."

Conde Naste and Advance Publications own, among many others, Reddit, Ars Technica, GQ, Vogue, Wired, and Epicurious. Advance Publications also owns literally dozens of major newspapers and websites, numerous television channels, magazines, and so on. Advance Publications has revenue of around $8,000,000,000 per year .

Reddit likes to try to play the "We're just a small completely independent company that somehow made it big, $4 of gold at a time!" but it's just marketing, and their position in the corporate hierarchy is something they go out of their way to conceal. That ars article I linked above is clear evidence of this as that is undeniably one of the most shameful "disclosures" ever, and in a article that's entire topic is the legal troubles of the CEO of their sister company.

From my interpretation, I think reddit.com users dismissed that pivotal event of repositioning reddit.com under a major publishing company naively thinking that change would have absolutely no effect on their beloved "free speech above all" platform. (I admit I wasn't paying enough attention myself at the time).

If anything, I think reddit.com can serve as a bad example of how to operate and grow a news aggregate/discussion website where users are supposed to come first.
